claims.text: Controlled chemical dealloying of a multielement precursor can produce three-dimensional noble-metal-based high-entropy-alloy nanoframeworks.
Chemical dealloying can enhance atomic mixing in the resulting NM-HEA.
The dealloyed NM-HEA nanoframework has enhanced catalytic properties.
The proposed precursor is a homogeneous mixture of noble metals and less-noble sacrificial elements.
The etchant preferentially removes less-noble elements from the precursor.
Controlling dealloying temperature and time preserves the integrity of the remaining high-entropy framework.
Removal of sacrificial elements induces an interconnected three-dimensional porous nanoframework.
The remaining noble metals retain an atomic-scale random distribution during nanoframework formation.
Selective etching triggers nanoscale reorganization of the residual alloy.
Nanoscale reorganization produces a high-surface-area porous structure with precise atomic mixing.
The porous, atomically mixed structure optimizes catalytic surface sites.
The resulting NM-HEA has a three-dimensional porous architecture.
The nanoframework provides greater active-site accessibility than conventionally synthesized dense HEA nanoparticles.
The nanoframework exhibits significantly better catalytic performance than conventionally synthesized dense HEA nanoparticles.
Conventional synthesis produces dense or agglomerated HEA nanoparticles with less-controlled structures and lower accessible surface areas.
Excessive etching can cause framework collapse.
Insufficient etching can cause incomplete porosity formation.
Changes in precursor composition can affect process reproducibility.
Chemical dealloying is an established method for fabricating nanoporous metals.
Atomic control and compositional uniformity in dealloyed NM-HEAs are sensitive to processing parameters.
